evidence.text:
Matched Coupling of Propargylic Carbonates with Cyclopropanols
Penglin Wu, † Minqiang Jia, *,† Weilong Lin, ‡ and Shengming Ma *,†,‡
†Research Center for Molecular Recognition and Synthesis, Department of Chemistry, Fudan University, 220 Handan Road, Shanghai
200433, P. R. China
‡State Key Laboratory of Organometallic Chemistry, Shanghai Institute of Organic Chemistry, Chinese Academy of Sciences, 345
Lingling Lu, Shanghai 200032, P. R. China
*S Supporting Information
ABSTRACT: The ring opening −coupling reaction of cyclopropanols with propargylic carbonates a ﬀording synthetically
attractive allenyl ketones has been developed. The mechanism involves the ligand-exchange reaction of in situ formed allenyl
palladium methoxide with cyclopropanols followed by carbon −carbon bond cleavage and reductive elimination. The reactions
proceeded smoothly under mild reaction conditions with Pd(0)/XPhos catalysis in the absence of any external base and
displayed a wide scope and application to a steroidal skeleton. The e ﬃciency of chirality transfer and synthetic utility of the allene
products have also been demonstrated.
T
he transition-metal-catalyzed coupling reaction of prop-
argylic alcohol derivatives with preformed organometallic
reagents such as organomagnesium, aluminum, zinc, borane, and
silane reagents have been extensively studied for the synthesis of
either alkynes and/or allenes 1−4 (Scheme 1 A). We envisioned
application to cyclopropanols, which are readily available from
Ti-catalyzed reaction of carboxylates with ethylmagnesium
bromide,5,6 as an equivalent to organometallic reagents to couple
with propargylic carbonates forming intermediate A to a ﬀord
allenyl ketone products.7 The challenges are the match of the C−
C bond cleavage reaction with the oxidative addition of
propargylic carbonates with palladium, the intrinsic readily
occurring β-H elimination a ﬀording α,β-unsaturated enone B
together with the corresponding reductive elimination product
allene C, and the possible formation of regioisomeric product
alkyne D (Scheme 1B). Here, we report our recent results on Pd-
catalyzed e ﬃcient and highly selective synthesis of allenyl
ketones.
Cyclopropanol 1a and propargylic carbonate 2a were taken as
the model substrates to test our hypothesis. After some trial and
error, toluene was the solvent of choice for this transformation.
Subsequently, di ﬀerent types of phosphine ligands were
screened. Unfortunately, Pd(dba)
2 and PPh 3 provided merely
13% yield of the desired allene product 3aa, and the B-type of β-
H elimination product enone 4′ and C-type of allene 3aa′ were
observed as the major products. In addition, an unexpected ring-
opening−protonolysis product, ethyl benzyl ketone 4, was also
formed (Table 1, entry 1).
When other ligands, such as PCy
3, rac-BINAP, LB-Phos, and
Gorlos-Phos, were used, the substrate 2a was recovered with
various amounts of the byproducts 3aa′, 4, and 4′ (Table 1 ,
entries 2−5). To our delight, when SPhos was used as ligand, the
corresponding allene product was generated in 58% yield,
although 3aa′ was also formed in 20% yield ( Table 1, entry 6).
Furthermore, changing ligand to XPhos provided 3aa in 78%

yield, and the formation of byproducts 3aa′, 4, and 4′ can be
suppressed to a very low level ( Table 1 , entry 7). Control
experiments showed that Cs 2CO3 could not improve either the
yield or selectivity of the reaction ( Table 1, entry 8). The results
with Pd(OAc) 2 and Pd(TFA) 2 were worse ( Table 1 , entries 9
and 10). Finally, the loading of Pd(dba) 2 and XPhos may be
reduced to 2.5 and 5 mol %, which even provided a slightly higher
yield of 3aa with a similar selectivity (Table 1, entries 11 and 12).
It should be noted that D-type alkyne product was NOT formed
in all cases.
With the optimized reaction conditions in hand ( Table 1 ,
entry 11), the generality of this reaction with the scope of
diﬀerently substituted cyclopropanols was investigated, and the
results are summarized in Scheme 2.D iﬀerent substituents, such
as Me and synthetically useful MeO, Cl, and Br on the benzyl
group could be tolerated, providing the corresponding 3,4-allenyl
ketone products 3aa−ea in 56−74% yields. The X-ray structure
of 3ea conﬁrmed the allene structure unambiguously (Figure 1).
8
Phenoxymethyl and 4-Cl- or 4-MeO-substituted aryl groups all
worked smoothly to provide the ﬁnal products 3fa, 3ga, and 3hb
in 71−72% yields. R 1 may also be di ﬀerent alkyl groups, such as
PhCH2CH2, n-hexyl, or cyclohexyl, delivering the desired allene
products 3ia−ka and 3jb in 70−74% yields.
Subsequently, di ﬀerent propargylic carbonates were also
investigated with cyclopropanol 1a (Scheme 3 ). R 2 may be
diﬀerent alkyl groups such as n-butyl, n-hexyl, and PhCH 2CH2
(3ab−ad,7 6 −81% yields). Di ﬀerent functional groups such as
CC bond, chloro, ketone, ester, and cyano groups may all be
incorporated into R2 and R3 to provide the ﬁnal products 3ae−aj
in 55 −79% yields. In addition to these secondary propargylic
carbonates, tertiary propargylic carbonates may also be applied to
aﬀord the fully substituted allene products 3ak and 3al; however,
the reaction conditions had to be reengineered: K 3PO4·3H2O
should be applied and the reaction should be conducted at 80°C.
When R 2 = H, the corresponding disubstituted allene product
3an was also obtained albeit in a very low yield (20%).
Since some allenes bearing steroidal skeleton have been
showing pharmacological activities, 9 cyclopropanol bearing a
steroid unit 1l was applied under the standard reaction
conditions. To our delight, the reaction with two representative
propargylic carbonates 2a and 2d worked smoothly to provide
the corresponding allene products 3la and 3ld in high yields
(Scheme 4).
Furthermore, we studied the e ﬃciency of central to axial
chirality transfer by applying optically active chiral propargylic
carbonates ( R)-2e,( R)-2g and ( R)-2m (Scheme 5 ). The
corresponding chiral allenes were generated smoothly with
high er. The absolute con ﬁguration of the product was
determined by X-ray crystal structure of enantiopure ( R)-3am
(Figure 2).
10
The potential of this reaction was further demonstrated on
gram-scale synthesis of the allene product 3db in 75% yield. This
allene product 3db may be subjected to various types of
transformations, such as reduction of the ketone group with
NaBH
4 providing the secondary alcohol 5, 1,2-addition of the

ketone group with EtMgBr or alkynyl lithium reagent generating
the tertiary alcohols 6 and 7, and reductive amination yielding
allenyl amine 8. The one-pot reduction-Au(I)-catalyzed
cyclization was also conducted providing the trisubstituted
tetrahydrofuran derivative 12 in a decent yield (Scheme S1 in the
SI ﬁle).
To shed some light on the reaction mechanism, several control
experiments were carried out ( Scheme 6 ). First, when cyclo-
propanol 1a was submitted to the standard conditions, 1a was
recovered in 84% yield together with 6% of ring opening
protonolysis product 4, and β-H elimination product 4′ was not
observed, indicating that most likely the reaction did not start
with 1a (Scheme 6, eq 1). Second, when carbonate2a was treated
with ethanol instead of cyclopropanol 1a, both alkyne 9a and
allene 3aa′ were formed respectively, as a mixture, indicating the
unique eﬀect of the cyclopropanols on the high selectivity for the
exclusive formation of allene. Although a very slow reaction was
observed when tert-butyl alcohol was used, both9a and 3aa′ were
detected with a similar ratio as with EtOH as judged by
1H NMR
analysis and isolation; thus, steric e ﬀects were not the major
reason for the high selectivity of allene over alkyne (Scheme 6,e q
2).
Finally, the coupling of propargylic acetate 10a with 1a was
found to be not only quite sluggish but also to yield the related
allene product 3aa in only 26% NMR yield together with 35%
NMR yield of ketone 4 and 24% of 10a, which highlighted the
importance of the carbonate for the high selectivity of this
coupling reaction matched reactivity of carbonates with the ring-
opening reaction of cyclopropanols ( Scheme 6, eq 3).
On the basis of these results and the stereochemical outcome
of the chirality transfer shown in Scheme 5 ,ap l a u s i b l e
mechanism is proposed ( Scheme 7 ): S
N2′-type anti-oxidative
addition of Pd(0) with propargylic carbonate2 would provide, by
eliminating a molecule of CO 2, the allenyl palladium methoxide
intermediate I, which would undergo ligand exchange with
cyclopropanol 1 providing the intermediate II. Subsequent ring

opening reaction of the three-membered cycle involving a β-C
elimination would yield intermediate III, which would undergo
reductive elimination to deliver the ﬁnal product 3 and
regenerate the Pd(0) species to complete the catalytic cycle.
We reason that the steric bulkiness of the ligand (XPhos)
prevents intermediate III from β-H elimination and facilitates the
subsequent reductive elimination, thus, avoiding the formation of
B- and C-type of products shown in Scheme 1.
In conclusion, a palladium-catalyzed highly selective and
eﬃcient synthesis of allenyl ketones via the matched oxidative
addition of propargylic carbonates with Pd(0) and the ring
opening of cyclopropanols has been developed. The reaction
features mild reaction conditions and a wide substrate scope
without using any air sensitive metal reagents or external base,
allowing the e ﬃcient introduction of the allene unit into useful
organic skeleton including even the steroidal skeleton. The high
eﬃciency of chiral transfer and synthetic utility of the 3,4-allenyl
ketone products were also demonstrated.
